title: My First Week at University
paragraphs: Monday. Today was my first day at the University of Panama. I woke up at five because the bus to the campus takes an hour. I was so nervous that I didn't eat breakfast. The campus is huge, and I got lost twice before I found my classroom.
Tuesday. I met two classmates, Kevin and Ariana. We have the same Economics class, and we sat together at lunch. The cafeteria is cheap: a big plate of rice and chicken costs only three dollars.

Wednesday. My English teacher gave us a lot of homework. We have to read a short article and write a summary, and I've never written a summary in English. I stayed in the library until seven o'clock, but I finished it.
Friday. What a week! I'm tired, but I feel more confident now. I'm still learning how the bus system works, and I'm going to buy a travel card on Monday. Tomorrow I'm going to sleep until noon!

title: Heavy Snow Surprises Bariloche
paragraphs: On Saturday morning, a lot of snow fell on Bariloche, in the south of Argentina. Nobody expected it, because the forecast said light rain. By ten o'clock, the snow was thirty centimetres deep.

Many tourists were having breakfast in their hotels when the lights went out for two hours. Others were driving to the ski centre, and they had to stop because the road was closed. 'We were listening to music when we saw the first snowflakes,' said Marcos Díaz, a visitor from Rosario.

Local workers cleared the main roads by midday. The ski centre opened in the afternoon, and more than two thousand people went up the mountain. A hotel gave free hot chocolate to everybody who was waiting in the lobby.
The weather service says that the snow is going to stop on Monday. Then the temperature will go up, and the roads will be open again. Tourists should check the news before they travel.

title: Come to Oaxaca with Us!
paragraphs: Hi Fernanda,
Guess what? Daniela and I are going to Oaxaca next month, and we want you to come with us! We're leaving on Friday the 14th, and we're coming back on Monday night.
We're taking the night bus from Mexico City. A ticket costs 780 pesos each way, and the journey takes about six hours. I'm booking the tickets on Wednesday, so please tell me before then.

We're staying at a small hostel in the centre. A bed in a shared room costs 250 pesos a night. On Saturday, we're visiting the market and taking a cooking class to learn how to make mole. On Sunday, we're going to a village where they make beautiful pottery.

I know you don't like waking up early, but the bus arrives at six in the morning. You can sleep on the bus, and then we can have a big breakfast together. Please say yes! It won't be the same without you!
Write back soon,
Paula

title: Why Teenagers Need More Sleep
paragraphs: Do you often feel tired at school? You are not alone. Many teenagers sleep too little, and this is a serious problem.

Doctors say that people between fourteen and eighteen need eight to ten hours of sleep every night. However, a lot of students sleep only six or seven hours. They stay up late with their phones, and they wake up early for classes.

Sleep isn't only about energy. When you sleep, your brain organises what you learned during the day. If you don't get enough sleep, you can't concentrate well, and you forget things more easily. You may also feel angry or sad for no reason.

Here are a few easy tips. First, stop using your phone an hour before bed. Second, don't drink too much coffee or cola in the afternoon. Third, go to bed at the same time every night, even at the weekend. After a week, you will probably feel much better.
Remember: a good night's sleep is as important as a good breakfast.

title: Four Months as a Volunteer in Kenya
paragraphs: Beatriz Salas, twenty-one, from Lima, spent four months in Nairobi, Kenya, in a tree-planting project. She is back home now, and she answered our questions.
Interviewer: Why did you choose Kenya?
Beatriz: I wanted to see a different part of the world. I also wanted to improve my English, because in Nairobi people speak English and Swahili.
Interviewer: What did you do every day?
Beatriz: We woke up at six and took a truck to the hills. We planted about two hundred trees a week. It was hard work, and my hands hurt a lot at the beginning.
Interviewer: What was the biggest surprise?
Beatriz: The people! Everybody was so friendly. My host family invited me to a wedding, and I danced for three hours. I also learned to cook ugali, a thick dish made with corn.
Interviewer: Would you go again?
Beatriz: Definitely. Next year, I'm going to apply for another programme in Tanzania. My advice to young people: don't wait for the perfect moment. Just go!

title: The Night the Laptop Died
paragraphs: Mariana had an important presentation on Monday morning. On Sunday night, she was finishing her slides when her laptop suddenly went black. She pressed the power button again and again, but nothing happened.

She called her brother, Esteban, who studies computing. 'Don't panic,' he said. 'Maybe it's only the battery.' He came to her house at ten o'clock and checked everything. 'It isn't the battery,' he said. 'It's the hard drive, and I can't repair it tonight.'
Mariana felt terrible. Her slides were online, so she could open them on a different computer. But she didn't have another computer, and the internet café near her house was closed.
Esteban had an idea. He called his friend Rodrigo, who lives two streets away. Rodrigo lent them his old laptop, and Mariana worked until two in the morning.

On Monday, her presentation was excellent, and her teacher gave her the best mark in the class. The next day, she bought a new laptop for 4,500 quetzales. Now she saves every file in two places, and she never works without a backup.

title: Three Weeks in Bolivia on a Small Budget
paragraphs: Last summer I travelled around Bolivia for three weeks with my friend Gabriel. We didn't have much money, but we had an incredible time. Here are my best tips.
Tip 1: Use local buses. A bus from La Paz to Sucre costs about 120 bolivianos, and it is much cheaper than a plane. The journey is long, so bring a jacket, some snacks and a good book.
Tip 2: Eat where the locals eat. In the markets, a big lunch with soup and chicken costs only 15 bolivianos. We ate there almost every day, and we never got sick.
Tip 3: Be careful at high altitude. La Paz is very high, and on our first day we felt dizzy and had headaches. Drink a lot of water, walk slowly and try coca tea, which helps many people.

Tip 4: Book hostels early in July, because they are full of tourists. Our favourite was in Uyuni: it was cheap and clean, and it had really good showers. The best part of the trip was the salt flat. It's the most amazing place I've ever seen.

title: How to Open a Savings Account
paragraphs: Do you have your first job or some money from your family? A savings account is a safe place to keep it. In Ecuador, you can open one in about thirty minutes.
Step 1: Choose a bank. Compare at least three. Look at the monthly fee and the places where you can take out cash.
Step 2: Bring your documents. You need your identity card, a recent bill with your address and about ten dollars for your first payment. If you are under eighteen, a parent must come with you.
Step 3: Fill in the form at the bank and sign it. A bank worker will ask a few questions about your job and your plans. Answer honestly.
Step 4: Wait for your card. It normally arrives in one week. Then download the app, choose a strong password and don't share it with anybody.
Tip: Save a small amount every month. Even five dollars is a good start. Don't spend your savings on things you don't need.

title: Review: Casa Colibrí Hostel
paragraphs: Casa Colibrí Hostel, Oaxaca – 5 stars out of 5
I stayed at Casa Colibrí for four nights in July, and I'm already planning to go back. I travelled alone, and I was a little worried, but the staff made me feel at home from the first minute.

The location is perfect. It's only ten minutes on foot from the main square, and there are many cafés and shops nearby. My bed, in a room for six people, was comfortable, and I had a small locker for my things. Every bed has a light and a plug, which is very useful.

The best part is the roof terrace, where you can have a free breakfast every morning. They serve fruit, bread, beans and delicious coffee. In the evening, the hostel organises a free walk or a cooking class, and I met travellers from Germany, Korea and Brazil there.
There are a few small problems. There are only two showers for twenty guests, so the hot water finishes quickly in the morning. Also, the wifi doesn't work well on the second floor.
A bed costs 280 pesos a night. It's more expensive than other hostels, but it's worth it. I strongly recommend it.

title: Valparaíso: A City Painted on Its Walls
paragraphs: Valparaíso, in Chile, is famous for its colourful hills and its street art. When you walk through the streets, almost every wall has a painting. Some are small and funny, and others cover a whole building.

In the 1970s, painters began to use the city's walls to show their ideas. Later, young artists started to use spray paint, and they created a new style. Today, the city has hundreds of murals, and many of them were painted by local artists.

Not all the paintings are legal, but the city now helps artists. Neighbours can ask for a free mural on their wall, and a team of artists paints it in a few days. Many paintings were made to make the city more beautiful and to tell stories about its people.
Tourists can join a free walking tour every morning at ten o'clock. The guides explain who painted each mural and what it means. A tour takes about two and a half hours, so wear comfortable shoes.
If you visit, don't forget your camera. The best time for photos is in the late afternoon, when the light is warm and the walls look golden.
